headline: CRUDE DROPS 4%; GRAINS SOFTEN ON GOOD CROP NEWS
subheadline: Energy leads the complex lower while Belt crop reports keep weather premium out of corn and beans.
lead: Crude fell hard, off $3.35 to $77.89, the biggest single-session drop in weeks as Iran-Hormuz tensions, with the Strait of Hormuz premium that built since early April now deflating on diplomatic progress, keep unwinding. Grains drifted lower in sympathy: beans gave back 14 cents, corn 3.75. The reason is sitting in the crop reports: Missouri ahead of schedule, Minnesota corn and beans at 75% good-to-excellent, Michigan got its million-dollar rain.
the_takeaway: Crop tour week is pricing a good crop, not a great worry.
teaser: Belt crop reports say no weather premium. Crude's drop says oil risk is easing. Wait for Thursday exports.

one_number.context: Minnesota's crop reporting at 75% good-to-excellent, with corn 5% dented against a 2% five-year average, tells you the Belt is running ahead of the calendar. That removes the last credible weather-premium argument heading into Pro Farmer crop tour week.

yesterdays_call.summary: Called soybeans down, toward $11.59. Beans closed today at $11.59, exactly at the target level.
yesterdays_call.note: The level printed but beans got there on crude's coattails and crop-report pressure, not a standalone bean story. Call it played out on the number; the driver was right even if the thesis was shared with the whole complex.

sections.title: Grains Soften on Good Belt
sections.body:
- Soybeans gave back **14 cents** to $11.59, the biggest single-day pullback since the early-August reset, as Missouri crops running ahead of schedule and Michigan's four-inch rain event both hit the wire before the open.
- Corn slipped 3.75 cents to $4.47, relatively orderly given the energy-led selloff; the December contract at $4.70 tells you new-crop is holding a small premium but not adding one.
- No weather story to buy: the 6-to-10-day outlook calls for above-normal temps but the rainfall coverage is there, and Pro Farmer crop tour opening reports are pricing yield, not risk.
sections.catalyst: Missouri crops ahead of schedule; Minnesota 75% good-to-excellent; Michigan 4-inch rain reported.
sections.bottom_line: Pro Farmer tour week is building a bear case in the field, not a bull case at the desk.
sections.vs_yesterday: Grains: yesterday's quiet drift became outright selling on crop field reports.

sections.title: Wheat Breaks; Yesterday's Call Missed
sections.body:
- Chicago wheat lost 7 cents to **$6.43**, moving with the grain complex rather than holding its quiet firmness from Monday.
- The 6-to-10-day forecast calling for above-normal heat from the central Plains into the Ohio Valley is a factor to watch, but it did not hold wheat up today.
- No fresh export demand emerged to interrupt the pullback; the Senate farm bill markup scheduled for Thursday is the next policy event that touches wheat indirectly via crop insurance provisions.
sections.catalyst: Broad grain selloff on Belt crop news; no offsetting export catalyst.
sections.bottom_line: Wheat's line to watch is $6.40; a close below there says the range is breaking lower.
sections.vs_yesterday: Wheat: Monday's quiet firmness reversed completely today.

sections.title: Energy Leads the Complex Lower
sections.body:
- WTI crude fell to **$77.89**, off $3.35, as Iran-Hormuz tensions, with the Strait of Hormuz premium that built since early April now deflating on diplomatic progress, continue to unwind; Saudi Aramco reporting a 33% profit gain actually confirmed the premium is normalizing, not escalating.
- Natural gas dropped to $2.70, down 2.4%, sitting at just 4% of its 52-week range; inputs are getting cheaper, which is a tailwind for fall fertilizer bookings but not a price catalyst for crop futures today.
sections.catalyst: Iran-Hormuz premium unwinding; Saudi Aramco Q2 results confirm re-sold off exports offset constrained Strait flows.
sections.bottom_line: Cheaper crude is a fall input cost win; it is also a macro risk-off signal worth watching.

sections.title: Livestock Quiet; Milk Firms
sections.body:
- Live cattle and feeders each gave back 0.2%, landing at **$231.40** and $343.00 respectively; technical pressure from Monday carried through with no fresh packer news on the ongoing Cargill Fort Morgan lockout that began May 19.
- Lean hogs slipped 1.4% to $83.65, continuing the grind lower from the July high; Tyson's report of a $500-650M projected beef segment operating loss for 2026 is not bullish for packer bids.
- Class III milk moved the other direction, up 0.9% to $17.25 and now at 80% of its 52-week range; whole milk sales grew in 2024 per USDA ERS data, and that structural demand story is quietly working in dairy's favor.
sections.catalyst: Tyson Q3 beef segment loss guidance; ERS whole milk sales data; Cargill lockout ongoing with no resolution.
sections.bottom_line: Dairy is the one livestock contract adding value today; cattle is holding a floor, not building one.

outside_the_pit.title: Senate Ag Committee to Mark Up Farm Bill This Thursday
outside_the_pit.body: Chairman Boozman's revised text includes year-round E15 sales and delays state SNAP cost-share requirements. Markup Thursday means corn ethanol demand provisions and crop insurance text could shift before markets open Friday.

outside_the_pit.title: US Cropland Average Tops $6,000 per Acre for First Time
outside_the_pit.body: USDA data puts average cropland value above $6,000 per acre in 2026, with pastureland at $2,000. For producers thinking about expanding or refinancing, the collateral picture looks strong even as commodity prices soften.

weekly_thread.question: Will Pro Farmer crop tour data add a weather premium back into corn and beans, or confirm the Belt is on pace?
weekly_thread.status_text: Tuesday's field reports from Missouri, Minnesota, and Michigan all say the Belt is on pace. The crop tour is pricing yield, not risk, so far.

the_more_you_know.title: What Tyson's Beef Loss Means for Packer Bids
the_more_you_know.body: Tyson projecting a $500-650M beef operating loss for 2026 is not a cattle supply story, it is a margin story. Packers losing money on the box side have less room to bid up live cattle. With the Cargill Fort Morgan lockout already tightening capacity, the next fed trade negotiation has two headwinds: a distressed packer and a constrained kill floor. Watch the Wednesday noon boxed beef report for confirmation.

watch_list.desc: Weekly export sales: soybeans under 300K MT keeps the chart in charge; above 500K MT would be the first real demand signal since China's $17B commitment announcement.
Farm bill markup: year-round E15 language is the corn demand clause to watch; if it survives markup, add a small ethanol premium to new-crop corn.

watch_list.time: All week, Pro Farmer crop tour
watch_list.desc: Crop tour yield estimates: corn yield projections below 178 bu/acre nationally would be the first real weather-premium catalyst. Above 180 locks in the current selloff trend.
Boxed beef cutout: if choice drops below $310 with the Cargill lockout ongoing, packer bids on live cattle will soften further.

daily_quote.text: A wise man changes his mind, a fool never will.
